---
title: "How this was verified"
subtitle: "Provenance, audit protocol, and what the verdicts do and do not mean"
---

## Where this material came from

This catalog is derived from a set of deep-research documents produced by a large language
model (ChatGPT deep research) in July 2026, covering open methodological problems in indirect
treatment comparisons, population-adjusted indirect comparisons, component methods, and
quantitative bias analysis.

That origin is the reason this page exists. A machine-generated research agenda is a
plausible-sounding artifact whether or not it is correct, and publishing one as settled fact
would be a disservice. **Nothing from the source documents appears on this site without a
verification verdict attached**, and the evidence behind each verdict is shown on the entry
itself.

The source documents are kept as working material and are not published here.

## What was checked mechanically

Before any of the substantive audit, every resolvable identifier in the corpus was checked
against its registry.

| Check | Method | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Digital object identifiers | CrossRef API, matching first author, year, and title | 64 of 64 resolved correctly |
| Preprints | arXiv metadata | Both resolved with matching titles |
| PubMed identifiers | NCBI E-utilities | All resolved with matching titles |
| R package versions and publication dates | CRAN database | All exact, including four packages released in 2026 |
| Open-source development claims | GitHub API | Verified, including a pull request correctly described as open and unmerged |
| Numeric claims spot-checked against abstracts | PubMed | Exact, including a three-figure bias-reduction sequence |

The conclusion from that pass shaped everything after it. **Fabricated citations are not the
failure mode of this corpus.** The claims are attached to real papers with real numbers. The
risks that remained were subtler: a real paper cited for a claim it does not quite make, a
problem described as open that the literature has partly closed, a severity claim pitched too
strong, and claims about a software package that had moved on since the report was written.

## The audit

Every problem carries a set of atomic, falsifiable claims extracted from the source. Those
claims, not the prose around them, are what was tested.

### Literature verification

For each problem, an agent with web and PubMed access checked that each cited work actually
supports the claim attributed to it, and searched for later work that would resolve or narrow
the problem.

### Adversarial refutation

A second agent was instructed to *refute* the proposition that the problem is open, and to
default to "not open" when uncertain. Asking an agent to confirm a claim and asking it to
break the claim produce different results; only the second is informative.

### Independent external auditors

Two frontier models outside this system were given the same claims, blind to each other and
to the verdicts above:

- **GPT-5.6 Sol** at maximum reasoning effort, via the `codex` CLI
- **Grok 4.5** at high reasoning effort, via the `grok` CLI

Both were constrained to answer from their own knowledge of the evidence-synthesis and causal
inference literature, and asked to return a graded verdict, a reason, and any counterevidence.

**Coverage was not equal, and that matters.** Grok's usage balance was exhausted partway
through the run, so it reached only a fraction of the catalog. Entries it never saw carry two
independent opinions rather than three. This is recorded rather than smoothed over, because an
entry judged by two auditors is weaker evidence than one judged by three.

| Auditor | Entries covered |
|---|---|
| Literature and prior-art check (Claude) | 232 of 232 |
| GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens | 232 of 232 |
| Grok 4.5, recency lens | 47 of 232 |

### Checking the auditors

An audit is only worth what its auditors are worth, so their own load-bearing claims were
spot-checked by hand against primary sources. Every checked claim held: `marginal_effects()`
does exist in `multinma` 0.7.0, `nmathresh` is on CRAN, the Behaviour Change Intervention
Ontology papers resolve, and Ishak et al. 2025 in *PharmacoEconomics* is real. No invented
locator, version number, or function name was found.

One auditor finding is worth stating on its own, because it changed several entries: the
source report proposes a reporting and credibility standard for population-adjusted indirect
comparisons without citing
[Ishak et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1), which published one.

Using two auditors rather than one is the point. On a pilot run they agreed that a claim about
the emptiness of the quantitative bias analysis literature was overstated, both citing the
mature epidemiological bias-analysis toolkit. On a different claim, about whether
cross-subnetwork component constancy is testable at all, **they disagreed** — and the
disagreement was substantive rather than noise. Where auditors disagree, this site shows the
disagreement rather than resolving it silently.

### Code verification

Problems that describe limitations of a specific software implementation were re-checked
against that package's current source, not against the report's description of it. Some had
already been fixed; those are marked as resolved rather than deleted, because the underlying
methodological problem is still worth recording.

### Adjudication

Verdicts follow a fixed rule, applied to the evidence gathered above:

| Condition | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Later work resolves it, in the literature or in code | [Resolved since report]{.verdict .verdict-resolved-since-report} |
| At least two of the three independent checks call it overstated | [Overstated]{.verdict .verdict-overstated} |
| All checks agree it is open and no counterevidence surfaced | [Confirmed open]{.verdict .verdict-confirmed-open} |
| Existing work covers part of it | [Partially addressed]{.verdict .verdict-partially-addressed} |
| Checks disagree, or evidence is insufficient | [Unverifiable]{.verdict .verdict-unverifiable}, with the dissent shown |
| No support could be found | [Not supported]{.verdict .verdict-not-supported} |

## Which fields are audited, and which are editorial

Not everything on an entry page is a verified claim, and the difference matters.

**Audited.** The statement, the reasons the problem is open, the cited prior work, and every
claim extracted from them. These went through the process above and carry the verdict.

**Editorial.** Maturity and tractability are *not* stated anywhere in the source material.
The source has no such fields; these values are a classification applied during extraction to
make the catalog browsable. They are one reader's judgment, they were not audited, and they
should not be cited as findings.

**Deliberately rebuilt.** Priority is not carried over from the source either. The source's own
master matrix grades 30 of its 46 rows "Very high" and 15 "High", which is under half a bit of
information and not usable as a ranking. Priority here reflects three observable things
instead: whether the problem blocks a decision-grade estimand, whether any method addresses it
at all, and whether any software implements it.

## What the verdicts do not mean

A verdict of [Confirmed open]{.verdict .verdict-confirmed-open} means the claim survived the
checks described above. It does not mean the problem is provably unsolved. Absence of
counterevidence in a targeted search is weaker evidence than a systematic review, and this was
not a systematic review: there was no protocol registration, no duplicate screening, and no
formal risk-of-bias assessment.

A verdict of [Overstated]{.verdict .verdict-overstated} is a refinement, not a dismissal. In
almost every case the underlying problem is real and the correction concerns how strongly it
was stated.

Model-based auditors have their own failure modes. They can be confidently wrong, they share
training data with the system that produced the source documents, and their knowledge has a
cutoff. They were used because two independent expert opinions are better than none, not
because they are authoritative.

**Where an entry matters to a decision, read the cited primary sources.** This catalog is a map
of where the problems are, and a record of how hard each claim was pushed on. It is not a
substitute for the literature it points to.

## Reproducing this

The site source, the build script, and the workflow definitions are in the
[repository](https://github.com/choxos/ITC-open-problems). Entry pages are generated from a
structured registry rather than hand-written, so the audit metadata on each page is the same
data the adjudication used.
